scene.title: Why six feet is the useful length
scene.summary: A defect in a long stick ruins a long stick.
scene.purpose: A defect in a long stick ruins a long stick.
narration: The members here are short, and that is not a compromise. A knot or a bend does not destroy wood; it destroys whatever length has to be thrown away around it.
That length is set by the piece you were trying to make. On a sixteen foot stick, one bad metre in the middle costs the whole board.
On six foot pieces it costs one piece. It also means a crooked farm tree is usable.
Cut the bend out at its middle, go six feet clear either side, and the sections above and below it are both still structure.
equations: short pieces, more places for a defect to fall
a bend costs one piece, not one board

scene.summary: A shell that did not care what shape its sticks were.

narration: Before any of this there was the frankendome. Forty triangles joined along their edges from the top down, and deliberately strut-agnostic: any section, any stock, whatever was to hand.

scene.lesson_title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
scene.title: The V bracket that made it possible
scene.summary: One connector that does not care what it is holding.
scene.purpose: One connector that does not care what it is holding.
narration: Edge-to-edge joining between odd-shaped members is a bracket problem, and most bracket types need to know what they are gripping before you can make them. A V bracket does not.

It folds to the corner angle and seats inside the vee between two struts, with long legs running down each one and the screws spread wide along that length. The spread is what stops the joint rotating, and because the bracket only ever touches the inside faces it does not care what section it has hold of.
That is exactly why the frankendome used it. I wanted to study how different trunk-harvested strut types behaved against each other, and this connector let me mix them freely.
It also scales by repetition. Need more corner?
Add another, longer bracket over the first. I built it that way knowing I could keep stacking them as the domes got bigger.
equations: folded from flat stock
any member type, same corner

scene.title: What holds the wedge dome together
scene.summary: Not brackets. These members are all alike, so the joint gets simpler.
scene.purpose: Not brackets. These members are all alike, so the joint gets simpler.
narration: The V bracket solves a problem the wedge build does not have. It exists to join unlike things, and every member here is the same shape as every other one.

So the joint gets to be simpler. Inside a triangle the members are glued on their mating faces and screwed in from the far side of the neighbour, so the fastening pulls the joint together rather than hanging off it.

Between triangles, the panels bolt to each other edge to edge, and the bolt can pass straight through one of the seam keys that was going in anyway. If I do end up wanting brackets on a wedge dome, they will have to change shape to suit it.
The frankendome's are the wrong tool for a frame this uniform.

panels bolted edge to edge through a key

scene.summary: The wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.

The way to read them is to look at a pair either side of one seam. The points can face into the dome together, out at the sky together, apart into their own panels, or in toward each other across the seam.
It costs nothing to choose. Same stick, same wood, turned before it goes down.
But the choice changes how deep the section is in the direction the shell actually bends.

scene.title: What the rotation is worth
scene.summary: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
scene.purpose: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
narration: A shell member is pushed in and out along the dome's own radius, so the stiffness that matters is measured in that direction. Turn the sector and the area does not move by a thousandth of an inch, because rotating a shape does not add wood to it.
The section modulus moves a great deal. Pointing the wedge at the centre of the dome, bark out at the weather, is the position that puts the most depth where the bending is.
It also puts the densest outer wood on the wet side and leaves both flat sawn faces where the seam key wants them.
